title: Meeting Rooms
directAnswer: A person can attend every meeting only if no two meetings overlap. Sort by start time, then check adjacent pairs: if any meeting starts before the previous one ends, return false. After sorting, the only meeting that can conflict with the current one is its immediate predecessor — so one linear scan suffices. O(n log n) sort, O(n) scan.

remember.pattern: Sort by start, check adjacent overlap
remember.formula:
meetings.sort(by start)
for i in 1..n-1:
    if meetings[i].start < meetings[i-1].end: return False
return True
rules: **Sort by start first.** Then overlaps can only be between neighbors — no need to compare all pairs.
Conflict test is `start[i] < end[i-1]` (strict `<`): a meeting that begins exactly when the prior ends is fine.
You want a boolean, not a merge — return false the instant you find one conflict.
Compare each meeting to the immediate predecessor in sorted order, not to a running 'max end'.
Empty or single-meeting input → trivially true.
whenToUse: 'Can one person/resource attend/handle ALL intervals?' yes/no question
Detect whether ANY two intervals overlap
You need a boolean, not a count or a merged set
antiSignals: 'How many rooms?' → max concurrency, min-heap or sweep (LC 253)
'Merge the overlaps' → sort by start, sweep-merge (LC 56)
'Remove fewest to make disjoint' → greedy by end (LC 435)
Endpoints are inclusive (a meeting [1,2] blocks another starting at 2) → use `<=`
remember.takeaway: When you only need to know IF intervals collide, sort by start and look at neighbors — a single adjacent overlap is enough to answer no. It's the lightweight cousin of Merge Intervals: same sort, but you short-circuit on the first conflict instead of building a merged list.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you realize sorting by start reduces 'do any two overlap?' from O(n²) pair-checking to a single neighbor scan.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Comparing every pair (O(n²)) instead of sorting, or getting the boundary wrong so a meeting starting exactly when another ends is flagged as a conflict.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Explain why adjacency-after-sorting is sufficient, use strict `<` for the touch-is-ok semantics, and note this is the warm-up to Meeting Rooms II where you count rooms instead of returning a boolean.

problemStatement:
Given an array of meeting time `intervals` where `intervals[i] = [startᵢ, endᵢ]`, determine if a person could **attend all meetings**.

A person can attend all meetings if and only if **no two meetings overlap**. Meetings that merely touch — one ending exactly when the next begins, like `[0,30]` and `[30,60]` — do **not** conflict.
constraints: A meeting ending at time t and another starting at t do NOT overlap
understanding: There's one person (or one room) and a list of meetings. The question is binary: can they make every single meeting? They can exactly when the schedule has no time conflict — no meeting overlaps another. Touching back-to-back is allowed.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does a meeting ending at time t conflict with one starting at t?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No — back-to-back meetings are fine. So the overlap test is strict: start < previous end.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the input sorted?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. I'll sort by start so I only have to compare adjacent meetings.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What should I return for an empty list or a single meeting?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: True — with zero or one meeting there's nothing to conflict with.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do I need to report which meetings clash, or just yes/no?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Just a boolean. That lets me return early on the first conflict found.

examples.explanation: [0,30] overlaps [5,10] (5 < 30) — the person can't be in two meetings at once.
Sorted: [2,4] then [7,10]. 7 ≥ 4, no overlap — all meetings attendable.
They touch at 30. Back-to-back is allowed, so no conflict.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Check Every Pair
approaches.whenToMention: Say it first to define 'overlap' precisely, then note it's quadratic and sorting fixes that.
hints: Two meetings conflict iff a.start < b.end AND b.start < a.end. What's the most direct way to check all of them?
Compare every unordered pair (i, j) with i < j; return false on the first overlap.
It's correct but O(n²). Is there an ordering that makes only neighbors worth comparing?
approaches.complexityReasoning: n(n−1)/2 pair comparisons in the worst case; no extra storage. Sorting cuts this to O(n) comparisons after an O(n log n) sort.
approaches.explanation:
The literal reading: a person can attend all meetings unless some two of them overlap, so check all pairs.

**The overlap definition.** Two meetings `a` and `b` overlap iff `a.start < b.end && b.start < a.end` — each starts before the other ends. Strict `<` encodes the 'touching is fine' rule. Loop over every pair and return false the moment one overlaps.

**Why we don't ship it.** With `n` up to 10⁴ that's ~50 million comparisons — passable, but it ignores structure. Sorting by start guarantees that if meeting `i` overlaps anything earlier, it overlaps meeting `i−1` specifically, so comparing all pairs is wasteful. State this, then sort.
approaches.insight: All-pairs checking is the honest baseline, but it throws away the fact that overlap is a *local* property once you order by time. Sorting turns a global pairwise question into a local neighbor question.

dryRun.intro: Check each pair with the two-sided overlap test; bail on the first conflict.

java.explanation: First half of the symmetric overlap test — i starts before j ends.
Second half — j starts before i ends. Both true ⇒ they overlap.

python.line: if intervals[i][0] < intervals[j][1] and intervals[j][0] < intervals[i][1]:
python.explanation: Two-sided strict overlap test; strict < lets back-to-back meetings pass.
Any single overlap means the person can't attend all — bail immediately.

edgeCases.behavior: Outer loop never runs → returns true (nothing to attend).
0 < 60 but 30 < 30 is false → not an overlap → returns true.

pitfalls: Using `<=` flips the touching rule and wrongly reports back-to-back meetings as conflicts.
O(n²) is needless when sorting gives O(n) comparisons.
Forgetting to return early — no need to keep scanning after the first conflict.

approaches.name: Sort by Start, Scan Adjacent (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The expected answer. Frame it as 'sort by start; the only possible conflict is with the previous meeting'.
hints: If meetings were sorted by start time, which earlier meeting is the only one that could still be running when the current one begins?
Sort by start. Walk from the second meeting; if its start is before the previous meeting's end, there's a conflict.
Return false on the first conflict; if you reach the end, return true.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Sorting is O(n log n) and dominates; the single neighbor scan is O(n). Sorting in place keeps extra space at O(1) (ignoring sort internals).
approaches.explanation:
Sort the meetings by start time, then scan once comparing each meeting to its immediate predecessor.

**Why adjacency is enough.** After sorting by start, the meetings are in non-decreasing start order. Suppose meeting `i` overlaps some earlier meeting `k < i`. Because starts are sorted, meeting `i−1` also starts no later than `i` and no earlier than `k`, and the earliest-ending relevant boundary to worry about is the one right before `i`. Concretely: if `meetings[i].start < meetings[i-1].end`, they overlap; if not, `i` starts at or after `i−1` ends, and since every earlier meeting ends no later than... — the cleanest framing is that once sorted, a conflict always shows up between *some* adjacent pair, so checking all adjacent pairs catches every conflict. No all-pairs loop needed.

**The conflict test.** `meetings[i].start < meetings[i-1].end` with strict `<`. Equality (`start == prevEnd`) is back-to-back, which is allowed. The instant the test is true, return false; if the scan completes, return true.

**Why a boolean, not a merge.** Unlike Merge Intervals, we don't build anything — we just need existence of a conflict, so we short-circuit on the first one. That's what keeps this an 'easy': same sort, simpler payload.
approaches.insight: Sorting localizes the question: 'do ANY two overlap?' becomes 'does any meeting start before its predecessor ends?'. The same sort-then-neighbor move underlies Merge Intervals — the difference is Meeting Rooms answers yes/no and stops early, while Merge builds the fused list. Recognizing they're the same skeleton makes both automatic.

pitfalls: Forgetting to sort — adjacent comparison is only valid on start-sorted input.
Using `<=` instead of `<` — flags valid back-to-back meetings as conflicts.

Comparing to a running max-end instead of the immediate predecessor (works, but unnecessary here; predecessor end is non-decreasing after sorting by start only if no overlaps — when overlaps exist you've already returned false).

commonMistakes: Checking all pairs in O(n²) instead of sorting and scanning neighbors.
Using <= so back-to-back meetings are wrongly counted as overlapping.
Forgetting that empty / single-meeting input must return true.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wrong boundary on touching meetings
commonMistakesDetailed.why: A meeting ending at t and another starting at t do not conflict. Using <= reports [0,30] and [30,60] as overlapping and returns false incorrectly.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
if intervals[i][0] <= intervals[i - 1][1]:   # flags back-to-back
    return False
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
if intervals[i][0] < intervals[i - 1][1]:    # touching is allowed
    return False

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Not sorting before the neighbor scan
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The adjacent comparison only catches all conflicts when meetings are ordered by start. On unsorted input a conflict can sit between non-adjacent entries and be missed.
